title: The mountain that bowed
hookLine: Vindhya grows to block the sun, and the Sri Yantra rises as Meru
carry: the holy sits at the center; the ego bows
tomorrow: what if the yantra were drawn on the one who reads it?
last: A ROAD THAT WORKS FROM EITHER END.

cards: At the center of the world, Hindu stories say, stands Meru, the golden mountain, and the sun circles it every day. In the Mahabharata, another mountain, Vindhya, grows jealous. Circle me too, it tells the sun.
When the sun refuses, Vindhya starts to grow, higher and higher, until it blocks the sun's road. The gods go to the sage Agastya, the same Agastya who asked for Lalita's names.
He asks Vindhya to bow so he can cross to the south, and to stay low until he comes back. The mountain bows. Agastya never comes back.

teach.h: AHAMKARA: THE EGO THAT WANTS THE CENTER.
teach.b: Many tellers read Vindhya as pride: ahamkara, the ego that wants the world to turn around it. Meru doesn't grab. It simply is the center, and the sun moves around it.

teach.h: THE HOLY IS THE TRUE CENTER.
teach.b: That's a big Hindu teaching: the self that insists on being the center blocks the light; the holy is the true center, and the ego is asked to bow. Now raise the Sri Yantra.
Lift the triangles above the petals, the petals above the rings, until it rises to a peak with the bindu at the top.

This raised form is called the Meru, and some worshippers keep one in metal or stone on an altar and worship it as they would the flat yantra. One of Lalita's names places her on the middle peak of Meru.

Look back down the mountain at the week: a lotus leaf that stays dry; Shiva and Shakti that won't come apart; a guru who guards and devotion that asks; every guardian greeted on the way in; Sri, the gift that pride drives away; all unfolding from the One and folding back.

teach.h: THE HOLY AT THE CENTER. THE EGO BOWS.
teach.b: All of it, now, a small mountain on a shelf, with her at the top.

how: Some Sri Vidya worshippers keep the Sri Yantra in its raised Meru form, in metal or stone, on a home altar or temple shrine, and worship it as they would the flat yantra; many Hindus end worship with a bow, forehead to the floor or to folded hands.

games.q: a friend says the Meru on Nani's altar is like a trophy: the higher you climb, the more you matter. what does the week's mountain say?
o: the summit is hers, not the climber's: the holy is the center, and the ego bows, like Vindhya.
right: the Meru is a reward kept by the most advanced worshippers.
it's only a shape; mountains in Hindu stories don't mean anything.
games.why: Meru is the center everything turns around; Vindhya, who wanted to be the center, had to bow. the summit of the raised yantra is the Goddess's seat.

practice: Sit tall, like a small mountain: a wide, steady base, the spine rising, the crown of the head light. Many Hindus end their worship with a bow, forehead to the floor or to folded hands.
When you're ready, bow your head slowly, like Vindhya letting the sun pass, and stay there for a few breaths. Then sit up, and rest.

wordCard.voice: The Sri Yantra, raised: the Meru, a mountain form of the same diagram, where going in is going up.

orig.note: Sanskrit Meru: the world-mountain of Hindu stories; the Sri Yantra's raised form.

carryVoice: One line to keep: the holy sits at the center; the ego bows. Vindhya is still bowing.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva: Vindhya grows to block the sun's path around Meru, and bows to Agastya, who never returns
Lalita Sahasranama, the name Sumerumadhyashringastha (she who is on the middle peak of Meru)
Sri Vidya tradition: the Sri Chakra in flat (bhu-prastara) and raised (meru-prastara) forms
